questiontext.text:
Goal

Add type annotations to a constant and four function signatures that already run without them.

How this works in Python

Every name in Java carries a type, and you write it before you write anything else.

int sensorId = 7;
String label = sensorLabel(sensorId, "RDR");
List<Double> readings = new ArrayList<>();
Map<String, Double> offsets = new HashMap<>();

static String sensorLabel(int sensorId, String prefix) { ... }
static void logFault(String name, String code) { ... }

Every topic before this one gave you none of that, and the omission was deliberate. A Java developer who keeps the declaration reflex writes Python that fights the language, so those topics took the crutch away and made you read a body to learn what a function wanted.

You asked whether real Python code carries types. It does, nearly everywhere. A modern codebase annotates every function it ships, and the safety-critical one you are about to join will be no exception. From this topic on, every signature in this course carries types, and so must yours.

An annotation is a type written into the source. Three places take one.

  • A parameter takes a colon and a type, so name: str says the argument is a string.
  • A return takes an arrow after the bracket, so def total(...) -> int: says the function hands back an integer.
  • A variable takes the same colon form, so count: int = 0 types the name as you create it.
def sensor_label(sensor_id: int, prefix: str) -> str:
    count: int = 0
    return f"{prefix}-{sensor_id}"

Container types use square brackets on the builtin, so list[int] is Java's List<Integer> and dict[str, float] is Map<String, Double>. Read the brackets as the diamond.

You will meet a second spelling in older files. typing.List[int] and typing.Dict[str, float] were the only forms available before Python 3.9, because the builtin list could not take brackets back then. It can now. The capital-letter forms are deprecated, so read them and never write them.

A value that may be absent is written with a vertical bar. float | None means a float or None, and it is the honest signature for anything built on .get() from the dictionaries topic. Java would hand you Optional<Double> or a bare nullable Double. Python 3.10 gave the bar its meaning, and the older typing.Optional[float] says the same thing in more characters. Write the bar.

A function that hands nothing back is annotated -> None. That is Java's void, and it is the one return type you might have been tempted to leave off.

What do annotations buy you? A type checker such as mypy, Pyright or Pyrefly reads them and reports the mismatches before the program runs. Point it at your file, or wire it into CI, and it will tell you that you passed a string where the signature promised an integer. That is the closest thing Python has to javac, and it is the reason production code annotates.

Two facts about annotations matter more than any of the syntax above. They are optional, so Python runs a file with none of them. And the interpreter ignores them, so it stores each one and then never looks at it again. Storage means you can read them back yourself.

print(sensor_label.__annotations__)
# {'sensor_id': <class 'int'>, 'prefix': <class 'str'>, 'return': <class 'str'>}

__annotations__ is a plain dict of the kind you built in the dictionaries topic, holding the real type objects. Every parameter is a key, and the return type is stored under the key return. The tests read that dict, so a missing annotation shows up as a missing key.

Your task

The code below already runs. Add the types and change nothing else.

  • READING_LIMIT is a module-level integer and takes a variable annotation.
  • sensor_label(sensor_id, prefix) takes an integer and a string and returns a string.
  • mean_reading(readings) takes a list of floats and returns a float. Annotate the local total as well, because a variable annotation is worth the same three characters here.
  • calibrate(offsets, name) takes a dict of string to float, takes a string, and returns a float that may be absent.
  • log_fault(name, code) takes two strings, prints a line, and returns nothing.

One display note before you start. __annotations__ stores None itself for a -> None return, so it prints as None. typing.get_type_hints() resolves the same annotation to the type of None and prints it as <class 'NoneType'>. Both describe the same signature.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Annotate every signature you write, every parameter and every return. A bare def header is a habit from the earlier topics and this tier ends it.
  • Write list[float] and dict[str, float]. The capital-letter typing.List form is deprecated, and a hidden test compares the stored objects, so it will catch you.
  • Write float | None. Optional[float] is banned, and the hidden test can tell the two apart even though Python calls them equal.
  • Import nothing. Your answer needs no typing module, and a test imports it for you where one is needed.
  • Add types and delete nothing. Every function below already passes its behaviour test, so breaking one costs you the whole question.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

expected.text: RDR-7 2.0 0.5 None FAULT rdr E14 None

testcode.text: import inspect import types assert sensor_label.__annotations__ == {"sensor_id": int, "prefix": str, "return": str}, "rule broken: annotate every parameter and the return" assert mean_reading.__annotations__["readings"] == list[float], "rule broken: write list[float], not the deprecated capital-letter form" assert calibrate.__annotations__["offsets"] == dict[str, float], "rule broken: write dict[str, float], not the deprecated capital-letter form" assert isinstance(calibrate.__annotations__["return"], types.UnionType), "rule broken: write float | None, not the older Optional spelling" assert log_fault.__annotations__["return"] is None, "rule broken: a function that hands nothing back is annotated -> None" assert __annotations__["READING_LIMIT"] is int, "rule broken: annotate READING_LIMIT" assert "total: float" in inspect.getsource(mean_reading), "rule broken: annotate the local total as well" print(len(sensor_label.__annotations__), len(mean_reading.__annotations__)) print(mean_reading([2.0, 4.0]), calibrate({}, "rdr"))
import typing print(typing.get_type_hints(calibrate)) print(typing.get_type_hints(log_fault)) print(READING_LIMIT + 1, sensor_label(1, "PWR"))

name.text: WAT 12.2: Brackets All the Way Down!

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write four annotated functions that group, total and flatten a sensor log, and find its busiest label.

How this works in Python

Java generics nest, and you read them from the outside in.

Map<String, List<Double>> byLabel = new HashMap<>();
List<Double> radar = byLabel.get("radar");
double first = radar.get(0);

Python spells the same shape with square brackets on the builtin, and it nests exactly as the diamond does. dict[str, list[float]] is that Map. Read it outside in and you get a dict, whose keys are strings, whose values are lists, whose items are floats.

by_label: dict[str, list[float]] = {}
readings: list[float] = by_label["radar"]
first: float = readings[0]

Nesting has no depth limit, so list[dict[str, list[float]]] is legal and describes a list of those dicts. Depth is a signal rather than a target. A signature three levels deep usually means the shape has earned a name of its own, and naming shapes is a job for a later topic.

Now the part Java has no word for. A tuple annotation comes in two shapes, and they mean different things.

pair: tuple[int, str] = (7, "radar")        # exactly two items, an int then a str
counts: tuple[int, ...] = (1, 2, 3, 4)      # any number of items, every one an int

tuple[int, str] fixes the length and the type of each position at once, so it is a Java record Pair(int id, String label) without the declaration. tuple[int, ...] fixes the type and leaves the length open, so it is Java's int[]. The three dots are a literal ellipsis you type, and they stand for nothing you left out.

Getting those two the wrong way round is the usual mistake. A function that hands back a count and a total returns tuple[int, float], a fixed pair of two known positions. A function that accepts however many readings turned up takes tuple[float, ...].

None of this pays for itself unless something reads it, and the thing that reads it is a type checker. A checker is a separate program rather than part of the interpreter. You run mypy . at your desk the way you run a test suite, and a CI job runs the same command and fails the build when it reports an error.

That is where the javac comparison earns its keep. The check happens on a machine before the code reaches a rig, which is the only kind of check that helps a safety-critical codebase.

Here is mypy on a list handed to something that wanted a dict.

station.py:19: error: Argument 1 to "busiest" has incompatible type "list[tuple[str, float]]"; expected "dict[str, list[float]]"  [arg-type]

Read it in five parts.

  • station.py:19 is the file and the line.
  • error is the severity, and a checker also emits note lines that carry no failure of their own.
  • Argument 1 to "busiest" names the called function and the argument position, counting from one rather than from zero.
  • has incompatible type A; expected B is always in that order, so the first type is what you wrote and the second is what the signature asked for.
  • [arg-type] is the error code. It is the string you search the documentation for, and the string you would name if you ever had to silence the check.

Pyright, the checker behind the editor squiggles in VS Code, reports the same mistake in its own words.

station.py:19:14 - error: Argument of type "list[tuple[str, float]]" cannot be assigned to
  parameter "groups" of type "dict[str, list[float]]" in function "busiest"
  (reportArgumentType)

Same file, same line, a column as well, the same two types in the same order, and a rule name where mypy puts an error code. Learn to read one and you can read the other.

One further complaint is worth meeting now, because a str | None return earns it every time.

station.py:20: error: Item "None" of "str | None" has no attribute "upper"  [union-attr]

The checker is telling you that one member of the union has no such attribute, so the call is unsafe for that member. It is the nag Java's Optional gives you by refusing to hand the value over, moved out of the type system and into a tool. Test for None before you use the value and the complaint goes.

Your task

Write four functions for a sensor log. A row is a label and one reading.

  • group_readings(rows) takes a list of pairs and returns a dict from label to the list of that label's readings, in the order they arrived. Build a plain dict with setdefault. An empty list gives {}.
  • tally(values) takes a tuple of however many readings and returns a fixed pair of the count and the total. An empty tuple gives (0, 0.0), and the total stays a float even then, so start it at 0.0.
  • busiest(groups) returns the label holding the most readings, or None when the dict has no labels at all. A label whose list is empty is still a label. The first label wins a tie.
  • flatten(groups) undoes group_readings and returns the list of pairs again, label by label.

Each function also builds one local container or running value, and each of those takes an annotation of its own. Four functions, four different bracket forms.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Write every bracket in full. dict[str, list[float]], never a bare dict and never the deprecated typing.Dict. A hidden test compares the stored objects, so it can tell the spellings apart.
  • A fixed shape gets tuple[int, float]. A variable length gets tuple[float, ...], ellipsis and all. Swap the two and the hidden test knows.
  • Annotate the container you build, not the signature alone. Four functions, four locals, four bracket forms.
  • Group with setdefault on a plain dict. defaultdict is banned here, because the return says dict and the printed form has to match what the annotation claims.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

testcode.text: LOG = [("radar", 1.5), ("power", 0.5), ("radar", 2.5), ("radar", 4.0), ("power", 1.5)] groups = group_readings(LOG) print(groups) print(group_readings([])) print(flatten(groups))

readings: tuple[float, ...] = (1.5, 2.5, 4.0) print(tally(readings)) print(tally(())) print(busiest({"radar": [1.5, 2.5, 4.0], "power": [0.5, 1.5]})) print(busiest({})) print(busiest({"radar": [], "power": []}))

import inspect import types assert group_readings.__annotations__ == {"rows": list[tuple[str, float]], "return": dict[str, list[float]]}, "rule broken: write every bracket in full, in the modern spelling" assert flatten.__annotations__ == {"groups": dict[str, list[float]], "return": list[tuple[str, float]]}, "rule broken: write every bracket in full, in the modern spelling" assert tally.__annotations__ == {"values": tuple[float, ...], "return": tuple[int, float]}, "rule broken: a variable length is tuple[float, ...] and a fixed pair is tuple[int, float]" assert busiest.__annotations__["groups"] == dict[str, list[float]], "rule broken: write every bracket in full, in the modern spelling" assert isinstance(busiest.__annotations__["return"], types.UnionType), "rule broken: write str | None, not the older Optional spelling" group_src = inspect.getsource(group_readings) assert "groups: dict[str, list[float]]" in group_src, "rule broken: annotate the container you build" assert "setdefault(" in group_src, "rule broken: group with setdefault on a plain dict" assert "defaultdict" not in group_src, "rule broken: group with setdefault on a plain dict" assert "total: float" in inspect.getsource(tally), "rule broken: annotate the running total as a float" assert "best: str | None" in inspect.getsource(busiest), "rule broken: annotate the answer so far as str | None" assert "rows: list[tuple[str, float]]" in inspect.getsource(flatten), "rule broken: annotate the container you build" count, total = tally((0.5,)) print(count, total) print(tally(())[1], type(tally(())[1]).__name__) print(busiest(group_readings([("aft", 1.0), ("fwd", 2.0), ("fwd", 3.0)]))) print(flatten({"fwd": [9.0]}))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write four annotated functions that show an annotation checking nothing at runtime and guards that do the checking instead.

How this works in Python

Hand two strings to a Java method that wants two integers and the build stops.

static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

add("1", "2");
// error: incompatible types: String cannot be converted to int

The class file never exists. The mistake cannot reach a test rig, let alone a flight computer. Every type you wrote in the first tier buys you that guarantee in Java, and the compiler enforces it before anything runs.

Now the same function in Python, annotated exactly as the first tier taught you.

def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b

print(add("1", "2"))   # 12

No error. No warning. The signature promised two integers and an integer back, and what actually happened was that "1" + "2" concatenated two strings into the string "12", which the function returned. The annotation said int and the value is a str.

This is the enforcement gap, and it is the most important thing in this topic. Annotations are inert at runtime. Python records each one in __annotations__ and then runs your code as though you had written none of them. Nothing is coerced. Nothing is rejected.

The type checker from the earlier tiers does the checking, and it runs at your desk or in CI, over the source. It never runs inside the running program. Draw the line there. A checker sees the values your source constructs, and it cannot see a value that arrives at runtime from a file, a socket, a message queue, a database row or a hardware bus.

For a safety-critical codebase that has one consequence worth writing on the wall. "We have type hints" is not "this input was validated". They are separate claims, and only the second one is a safety property. Reading an annotation as a guarantee about a runtime value is a real defect, and a review that accepts -> float as evidence that a float arrived has accepted nothing.

The repair is a boundary. Everything crossing into your program from outside gets an explicit check that raises. Everything inside stays annotated and unguarded, because the checker already covers the inside, and a guard on every call would cost you the speed that made the annotations free.

Two builtins do the work. isinstance(value, int) asks whether a value is an integer, and it is Java's instanceof. raise throws, as you saw in the exceptions topic.

if not isinstance(raw, str):
    raise TypeError(f"read_pressure needs a str, got {type(raw).__name__}")

Pick the error to match the failure. A TypeError means the wrong kind of thing turned up, so a list where a string was wanted. A ValueError means the right kind of thing carried an impossible value, so a pressure of 300 bar on a 250 bar line. Java splits these the same way with ClassCastException and IllegalArgumentException, and swapping them misleads whoever reads the log at 3am.

One trap is waiting, and the dictionaries and sets topic already showed you the cause. bool is a subclass of int, so isinstance(True, int) is True and a guard written with isinstance alone accepts True as the number 1. Where an integer means a count of fuel rods, that is not a value you want silently promoted. Reject bool with its own test before you accept int.

At a large boundary, an HTTP request or a queue message, production code often declares the shape once with a validation library such as Pydantic instead of writing the checks by hand. This exercise stays in the standard library so that you can see what such a library does for you.

Your task

Write four functions, all of them annotated.

  • naive_add(a, b) is the exhibit. Annotate it for two integers and an integer back, then leave the body as a bare return a + b with no checks at all.
  • lie_report() takes no arguments and returns a string. Call naive_add with the two strings "1" and "2", read the declared return type out of naive_add.__annotations__["return"] and take its __name__, take type(result).__name__ for what came back, and return declared int, returned str '12'. The quotes around the value come from the !r conversion you met in the strings topic.
  • checked_add(a, b) has the same signature and validates both arguments. It raises TypeError with the message checked_add needs an int for a, got str, naming the offending parameter and the type that turned up. Check a first, then b.
  • read_pressure(raw) takes a string and returns a float. Anything that is not a string raises TypeError with the message read_pressure needs a str, got NoneType. Convert the string with float(), annotate the result as a local variable, and raise ValueError with the message pressure 300.0 is outside 0.0 to 250.0 when the reading falls outside that range. Both ends of the range are allowed.

type(x).__name__ gives you the type name as a string, which is the same call you used in the dictionaries and sets topic. For None it gives NoneType.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Never trust an annotation to check anything at runtime. The only thing that checks a value is a line you wrote yourself.
  • Leave naive_add unguarded. It is the exhibit, not the fix, and a hidden test fails you for defending it.
  • Validate with isinstance and raise. assert is banned, because python -O deletes every assert in the file and takes your boundary with it.
  • Reject True where you want an integer. The dictionaries and sets topic told you bool is an int, so isinstance on its own is not a guard.
  • Wrong kind of thing raises TypeError. Right kind of thing, impossible value raises ValueError. Do not swap them.
  • Annotate all four signatures, the guarded ones included. Validating by hand is not a reason to stop writing types.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

expected.text: 7 checked_add needs an int for a, got str checked_add needs an int for a, got float checked_add needs an int for a, got bool checked_add needs an int for a, got NoneType 101.3 TypeError read_pressure needs a str, got NoneType TypeError read_pressure needs a str, got int ValueError pressure 300.0 is outside 0.0 to 250.0 ValueError pressure -1.0 is outside 0.0 to 250.0

testcode.text: import inspect assert naive_add.__annotations__ == {"a": int, "b": int, "return": int}, "rule broken: annotate every signature" assert checked_add.__annotations__ == {"a": int, "b": int, "return": int}, "rule broken: annotate every signature" assert read_pressure.__annotations__ == {"raw": str, "return": float}, "rule broken: annotate every signature" assert lie_report.__annotations__ == {"return": str}, "rule broken: annotate the return even with no parameters" naive_src = inspect.getsource(naive_add) assert "isinstance" not in naive_src and "raise" not in naive_src, "rule broken: naive_add stays unguarded, it is the exhibit" checked_src = inspect.getsource(checked_add) assert "isinstance" in checked_src and "raise TypeError" in checked_src, "rule broken: guard with isinstance and raise TypeError" pressure_src = inspect.getsource(read_pressure) assert "raise TypeError" in pressure_src and "raise ValueError" in pressure_src, "rule broken: wrong type raises TypeError, impossible value raises ValueError" assert "assert " not in checked_src + pressure_src, "rule broken: validate with raise, never with assert" print(checked_add(-2, 2), read_pressure("0.0"), read_pressure("250.0")) print(naive_add("safety", "critical")) try: checked_add(1, True) except TypeError as exc: print(exc)

expected.text: 0 0.0 250.0 safetycritical checked_add needs an int for b, got bool
